Field surveys of Pacific thread herring (Opisthonema libertate) in the eastern tropical Pacific indicate that sexually mature adults typically attain a maximum total length of 30 centimeters [Li = 30 centimeters], a size consistent with the moderate body plan characteristic of coastal clupeiforms. Growth increments slow markedly after individuals reach this upper boundary, with annual rings on scales suggesting that the oldest fish in the population approach a maximum lifespan of approximately 8 years [am = approximately 8 years] when maintained at a water temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This longevity is relatively extended for a small pelagic planktivore and may reflect the relatively stable thermal regime of the equatorial upwelling zones these fish inhabit.

Reproductive development in Opisthonema libertate proceeds steadily during the first year, and the total length at which 50 percent of individuals are expected to have completed gonadal maturation is 11.5 centimeters [Lp = 11.5 centimeters]. This length corresponds to roughly the second growing season for most cohorts, after which fish transition from juvenile foraging behavior to active participation in spawning aggregations. Puberty at this moderate size is typical among clupeids and allows young adults to commence breeding before they have achieved their full somatic dimensions, thereby lengthening the period available for lifetime reproductive output.

Under controlled laboratory conditions replicating the thermal conditions of the species' natural habitat, gravid females held at 27 °C [T = 27 °C] were observed to produce an average clutch size of roughly 313 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = roughly 313 eggs per spawning event] and a spawning frequency of about 0.5 events per day [F_R_i = about 0.5 events per day], culminating in a yearly output of approximately 57125 eggs. The high reproductive rate underscores the species' capacity for rapid population turnover in productive coastal waters.

The wet weight of a newly hatched yolk-sac larva is estimated at 0.00032 grams [Wwb = 0.00032 grams], a mass that reflects the small diameter of the fertilised ovum and the limited endogenous yolk reserves available before the onset of exogenous feeding. By the end of the yolk absorption stage, these larvae must successfully capture their first prey to sustain further growth, a critical bottleneck in early life history. In contrast, the ultimate wet weight achieved by fully grown adults reaches approximately 240.5 grams [Wwi = approximately 240.5 grams], representing a roughly 750,000-fold increase in mass from the larval stage through the juvenile and adult phases.

Comparing the extreme endpoints of the species' life cycle highlights the dramatic disparity in scale between early and late life. A neonate weighing just 0.00032 grams [Wwb = 0.00032 grams] must successfully navigate the pelagic larval phase, metamorphosis, and juvenile growth to eventually attain a mature body mass of 240.5 grams [Wwi = 240.5 grams]. At a sustained water temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the maximum documented lifespan is 8 years [am = 8 years], during which a female that commences reproduction at the pubertal length of 11.5 centimeters [Lp = 11.5 centimeters] may contribute hundreds of thousands of eggs to the spawning stock.
